newsitem.title: CANADA: Goodale to examine long-term grain solutions.
newsitem.headline: Goodale to examine long-term grain solutions.

text.p: Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale said on Friday he was willing to consider long-term solutions to ensuring Canadian grain gets to market but admitted he had little power in the short term.

Goodale told reporters he had seen some evidence in the week since he had met grain and rail representatives that grain was beginning to move more quickly, and said the players must "pull out all the stops."

But asked what he could do now, he said: "Well, there's very little at the federal level, quite frankly, because the system depends on the logistical performance of grain companies, railways, wheat board and others."

A shortage of locomotive engines and bad weather delayed the shipment of what Goodale said was 1.5 million tonnes of Canadian grain. Forty-four ships were waiting to load grain and oilseeds at Canada's Pacific ports on Wednesday.
A long-term solution would be for the grain and rail companies to build into their contracts rewards and penalties to prevent this from happening again, he said.
"In terms of the long term, I favor that idea and it's an idea I've talked positively about for a number of years," Goodale said.
"Wanting to have a system in which there are both rewards and penalties, there's a bonus for performance when the system actually delivers faster than expected and a penalty when the system falters."
The railway companies have said the shortage of locomotives is the result of existing tax laws that do not allow them to write off locomotives and rail cars.
"If the tax laws were changed today that wouldn't move any more grain tomorrow," he said.

"The argument might be made (that) it would make a difference next year or the year after that, and I'm prepared to have that conversation about the future, as others are prepared to have the conversation about penalties and incentives in the systems."
He added that it was neither physically or fiscally possible for the Canadian government to consider a compensation program.
In a sign of frustration with the delays, Canada's largest grain handler -- Saskatchewan Wheat Pool -- repeated its call for Goodale to use his influence.
"We need a system of accountability that will benefit all producers," stated the pool's president, Leroy Larsen.
"The industry is thousands of grain car unloads behind schedule and the West Coast is clogged up with vessels waiting for grain," he said.
"We can't wait. We need action now. We are losing customers and income at the farm level."
